lead: Propagation is the route a radio wave takes from the transmitting antenna to the receiving one. Below about 3 MHz a ground wave hugs the earth; from 3 to 30 MHz a sky wave goes up, is bent back by the ionosphere and lands hundreds or thousands of kilometres away; above 30 MHz a space wave travels in a near-straight line and needs line of sight. The frequency, the distance and the time of day decide which route works, which is why an AM station carries farther at night and an HF operator changes frequency at dusk.
prereq: You need: frequency bands and polarization from the antenna fundamentals topic.

blocks.text: Ground wave (surface wave): at LF and MF, roughly 30 kHz to 3 MHz, the wave travels along the surface, held by the conducting earth. It needs vertical polarization, because the earth shorts out a horizontal electric field. Its loss rises with frequency and over poor ground: it goes farthest over sea water and least over dry sand. AM medium-wave broadcasting and maritime radio use it.

Sky wave: at HF, roughly 3 to 30 MHz, the ionosphere refracts the wave back to earth, and one or more hops cover thousands of kilometres. It depends on the sun, the season and the time of day. Shortwave broadcasting, amateur radio and long-distance aviation HF use it.

Space wave: above about 30 MHz the ionosphere lets the wave through, so links rely on a direct ray (with a ground-reflected ray beside it) between antennas that can see each other. FM, TV, mobile networks, Wi-Fi, microwave hops and satellite links use it.

Solar ultraviolet and X-rays free electrons from the gas between about 60 and 400 km up. The refractive index of this plasma is n = √(1 − 81N/f²), with N in electrons per m³ and f in Hz, so n falls as N rises. A wave climbing into denser plasma bends away from the vertical and, if N is large enough, turns back down.

items: D layer, 60 to 90 km: daytime only; it does not return HF but absorbs MF and low HF, which is why medium-wave sky waves vanish by day.
E layer, 90 to 150 km: daytime refraction for MF and low HF, and occasional sporadic E.
F1, 150 to 250 km, and F2, 250 to 400 km: by day two layers, at night one F layer; F2 has the highest density and carries most long-distance HF.

blocks.where: f<sub>c</sub> is the critical frequency in Hz, the highest frequency a layer returns at vertical incidence; N<sub>max</sub> is the layer’s peak electron density per m³.

blocks.text: MUF is the maximum usable frequency of an oblique path; φ is the angle of the ray from the vertical where it meets the layer. This is the secant law.

For a flat-earth layer at virtual height h and a ground distance D between the stations, cos φ = h/√(h² + D²/4), so MUF = fc√(1 + (D/2h)²). Working the other way, a frequency f above fc cannot come down closer than the skip distance Dskip = 2h√((f/fc)² − 1). Between the end of the ground-wave range and the skip distance lies the skip zone, where neither wave is heard. Links are usually run at the optimum working frequency, about 0.85 × MUF, to leave room for changes in the layer. Fading comes from several rays arriving with changing path lengths, and from changes in the layer’s height and density.

sections.h3: Space waves and the radio horizon

blocks.text: The geometric horizon of an antenna h metres high is √(2R<sub>e</sub>h), with R<sub>e</sub> = 6371 km, which is 3.57√h km. Air density falls with height, so the refractive index falls too and the ray bends slightly downward, following the earth farther. The standard allowance replaces R<sub>e</sub> by 4/3 of itself, which gives the radio horizon:

blocks.where: d is the maximum line-of-sight range in km over a smooth earth with standard refraction; h<sub>t</sub> and h<sub>r</sub> are the transmit and receive antenna heights in metres.

blocks.text: Beyond the horizon, two effects can still carry a VHF to SHF signal: tropospheric scatter from irregularities in the lower atmosphere, weak but steady, and ducting, when a temperature inversion or a sharp moisture change, common over the sea, traps the wave in a layer and carries it far beyond the normal range, sometimes causing interference between distant stations.

examples.question: An F2 layer has a peak electron density of 1.24 × 10¹² m⁻³ and a virtual height of 300 km. Find (a) the critical frequency, (b) the MUF for stations 1000 km apart, and (c) the skip distance at 15 MHz.
steps: Optimum working frequency for the 1000 km link: 0.85 × 19.5 = 16.6 MHz.
examples.answer: f<sub>c</sub> ≈ 10.0 MHz; the MUF for 1000 km is about 19.5 MHz (work near 16.6 MHz); at 15 MHz nothing returns closer than about 668 km.

examples.question: A TV transmitter antenna is 100 m high and a rooftop receiving antenna is 9 m high. Find the radio-horizon range, and compare it with the geometric range. How far can a 25 m mobile tower reach a phone held 1.5 m above the ground?
steps: A 25 m mast alone (h<sub>r</sub> = 0) has a radio horizon of 4.12 × 5 = 20.6 km, against a geometric 17.9 km.
examples.answer: 53.6 km radio range (46.4 km geometric) for the TV link; about 25.6 km from a 25 m tower to a handset, though in practice path loss and buildings limit a cell long before the horizon.

traps: Writing MUF = f<sub>c</sub> cos φ. The secant law makes the MUF larger than f<sub>c</sub>: at φ = 60°, MUF = 2f<sub>c</sub>, not f<sub>c</sub>/2.
Calling the MUF the critical frequency. f<sub>c</sub> is for vertical incidence; the MUF belongs to one oblique path and is always at least f<sub>c</sub>.
Saying the D layer reflects HF. It absorbs by day; the F2 layer returns long-distance HF.
Using 3.57√h as the radio horizon. That is the geometric horizon; standard refraction gives 4.12√h, with h in metres and d in km.
Expecting a skip zone at frequencies below f<sub>c</sub>. Below f<sub>c</sub> even a vertical ray returns, so there is no skip zone.

quiz.q: Name the three propagation modes and a band for each.
quiz.a: Ground wave: LF and MF, about 30 kHz to 3 MHz. Sky wave: HF, 3 to 30 MHz. Space wave: VHF and above, from about 30 MHz.

quiz.q: Why does the D layer weaken daytime HF while F2 supports long-distance HF?
quiz.a: D is low and dense with molecules, so electrons collide often and turn the wave energy into heat. F2 is high, with many free electrons and few collisions, so it refracts HF back with little loss.

quiz.q: A layer has f<sub>c</sub> = 6 MHz. Find the MUF for a ray meeting it at 45° from the vertical.
Find the electron density that gives a critical frequency of 5 MHz.
Find the skip distance at 10 MHz for f<sub>c</sub> = 5 MHz and h = 300 km.

quiz.a: The ring of ground between the end of the ground-wave range and the skip distance, where neither the ground wave nor the sky wave arrives.

quiz.q: Why can an HF link fail at night on a frequency that works by day, while another works only at night?
quiz.a: At night the F-layer density and the MUF fall, so a high daytime frequency passes through. A low frequency absorbed by the D layer by day works at night, when the D layer disappears.

quiz.q: A coastal VHF link is strong some evenings and far-reaching enough to pick up distant stations. Suggest a cause and a test.
quiz.a: A temperature inversion over the sea forms a duct that traps the wave. Log the signal against time with weather data, or compare the received level at two antenna heights.

beyond: Not for the exam. HF users plan frequencies with ionospheric models fed by ionosondes, which sweep a signal upward and time the echoes to find f<sub>c</sub> and h. Above 10 GHz rain and gas absorption set satellite and 5G link margins, and ITU-R recommendations give the standard models. Search for ionosonde, ITU-R P.533 HF prediction and rain attenuation.

figure.caption: The sky-wave paths of the first worked example, with a flat earth and the F2 layer at 300 km. A ray meeting the layer 59° from the vertical lands 1000 km away, and needs a frequency no higher than the MUF of 19.5 MHz; at 15 MHz the steepest ray that still returns lands 668 km out, leaving a skip zone beyond the short ground-wave range.
